MR. SPENCER    REFERENCE TO INCIDENT DURING CALLING OF VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a question of privilege. Yesterday, following the taking of a vote of the house, your attention was directed by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mc-Ilraith) to the fact that one of the members of the house had left the chamber during the taking of the vote. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) identified him as chairman of the bill of rights committee, and indicated that he was leaving for the purpose of attending a meeting of that committee.
May I be permitted to say, in mitigation of the offence, that I was not leaving for any such purpose but that I had arranged to accept a long distance call at twenty minutes after two and left for the purpose of receiving that call. At the time it was arranged I had no idea that the division bells were going to ring so long that it would not be possible for me to register my vote on that motion and also accept that long distance call.
I extend to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house my apologies for offending against this rule of the house, and I hope that my apologies will be accepted by the members of the opposition in that respect.

maintopic: ONTARIO WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY- ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUPPORT PRICES

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: ONTARIO WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY- ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that in accordance with the requirements of the Agricultural Stabilization Act, which provides a mandatory stabilization or prescribed price at a minimum of 80 per cent of the base price for Ontario wheat, oats and barley, the agricultural stabilization board has established the base price for these commodities for the crop year July 1, 1960 to June 30, 1961.
The stabilization board has been authorized to provide a support price of $1.39 per bushel for Ontario wheat No. 2 Canada eastern grade or better quality, sold for milling or export purposes, basis on track at Ontario shipping points. This is the same prescribed price for Ontario wheat as last year, but is at approximately 82 per cent of the 10-year average or base price, which has been established as $1.70 per bushel, on track basis. The board, however, is authorized to determine the amount of any payments to producers on the basis of sales delivered at Ontario elevators, as was requested by the producers' association.
The 10-year average or base price for oats has been established at 71 cents per bushel, No. 2 Canada eastern grade or better quality, on track at Ontario shipping points. The prescribed price for the 1960-61 crop year will be at the 80 per cent mandatory level, which is 57 cents per bushel.
The 10-year average or base price for barley has been established at 99 cents per bushel, No. 2 Canada eastern grade or better quality, on track at Ontario shipping points. The prescribed price for the 1960-61 crop year will be at the 80 per cent mandatory level, which is 79 cents per bushel.

maintopic: ONTARIO WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY- ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture will recall that several times during the past six weeks he has been asked when he would be in a position to announce these prices under the Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act. The Ontario wheat farmers, through their appropriate agency, have been negotiating a price with concerned parties. On this account, it may have been the view of the minister that the announcement should not take place while such negotiations were under way. I am not aware that these negotiations have been completed.
In any event, the price of $1.39 for Ontario wheat, the prescribed price which the minister says is the same as last year, does not represent the price asked by the Ontario wheat grower. That price, I think, was in the neighbourhood of $1.60. There were certain other requests made by the Ontario wheat growers with which the minister has not dealt. However, if these negotiations are not complete one may draw the conclusion that the figure of $1.39 as compared with the asked price is not one calculated to assist the negotiations which are under way.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCORPORATE SECTION 273 OF RAILWAY ACT

speakeroldname: Mr. W. H. A. Thomas (Middlesex West) moved
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCORPORATE SECTION 273 OF RAILWAY ACT
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-87, to amend the National Energy Board Act (drainage works).

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCORPORATE SECTION 273 OF RAILWAY ACT
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCORPORATE SECTION 273 OF RAILWAY ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill seeks to amend the National Energy Board Act by incorporating into it section 273 of the Railway Act. When the National Energy Board Act was passed in 1959, sections 207 to 246 and section 248 of the Railway Act, which deal with the acquisition and expropriation of land for purposes of right of way, were included in the National Energy Board Act, but section 273 of the Railway Act which dealt with drainage was not included.
This amendment would make pipe lines operating under federal charter subject to provincial drainage laws in the same way as pipe lines which operate under provincial charter. Pipe lines involved in municipal drainage schemes would be treated like those of any other property owner. They would be subject to assessment for benefit, cost and damage like other properties, and their owners would enjoy the right of appeal to county or district courts for adjustment in such assessments. Owners of pipe lines would be made responsible for any added cost to a municipal drainage scheme caused by their presence.
The provisions contained in the proposed amendment were incorporated into the Railway Act in 1903 after an extended debate in parliament. It is suggested that the arguments which were valid and successful in connection with drainage problems caused by the railways in 1903 are equally valid today in connection with pipe lines.
This amendment is requested by Adelaide township in the constituency of Middlesex West. It is endorsed by Middlesex county council and by the Ontario association of land surveyors.

subtopic: PROTECTION FOR TOURISTS AGAINST MAULING BY BEARS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PROTECTION FOR TOURISTS AGAINST MAULING BY BEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources in reference to the national parks. There have been two serious incidents in which tourists in the parks, namely Banff and Glacier, have been badly mauled by bears, one incident where they were fishing at Spray lake and another incident at Glacier park. I was wondering whether the department had looked into the matter and whether any consideration is being given to changing

the regulations so that reliable people might carry firearms to protect themselves in situations of this kind.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: PROTECTION FOR TOURISTS AGAINST MAULING BY BEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad in a way that the hon. member for Bow River has raised the question of bears in the parks, because recently an increasing numbers of letters have been reaching my desk and the desk of the hon. member for Calgary South and other park members.
I should like to make it clear that under the National Parks Act it is my responsibility to protect the bears and in so doing we have worked out a policy under which we warn all the people who go into the parks about the danger of feeding bears. Since the tragic incident in 1958 in Jasper park we have established a new set of regulations for the treatment of bears in the parks. At the present time if any bear becomes too friendly along the highways we trap the animal and remove him to a very distant spot, and paint his rear end red. If this bear with the red posterior reappears in the settled areas where people are visiting the parks, then he is trapped a second time and removed permanently. This program was in effect in 1958 and 1959 and is in effect again this year, and quite a number of bears have been removed permanently.
I should like to make this one plea to those people who are interested in this matter. It is a very serious matter to those who attend the parks that the greatest culprits in these matters are those people who feed the bears and do not look after their garbage properly, because they are the ones who encourage the bears to come around human habitation which leads in the main to these tragedies.
In regard to the grizzly bears, which do not come near human habitation, they are not a real problem in Canada because they are quite remote. In the United States the grizzly bears are almost extinct, and the parks services are making a real effort to try to save the grizzly bears for the future. Therefore, in answer to the hon. member's question about the change in regulations, we have put into operation the regulations which I have described. Since we put them into operation there has been no serious or fatal accident in the parks.
As to the change in regulations concerning rifles, no consideration is being given to that at the present time.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Comtois (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED DROWNING ACCIDENT AT GREAT BEAR LAKE
speechtext:
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Mackenzie River asked me a question about two female employees of my department believed drowned in Great Bear Lake. I am sorry the hon. member is not in the house this morning because of serious illness, and I am sure everybody in this house wishes him a prompt recovery.
This is the report I have received. The girls, two geographers, Miss Joan Goodfellow, 27, and Miss Anne-Marie Kroeger, 35, were employed on a joint project of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the Arctic Institute of North America to investigate the raised beaches and related features of Great Bear lake as an aid to interpreting the glacial history of the region. Miss Kroeger had obtained a grant from the Arctic Institute of North America and had been authorized by the institute to undertake the survey. They were flown in to Great Bear lake from Edmonton on June 25 last. They were equipped with a 17-foot rugged freighter canoe, the regular issue for the type of country in which they were working. With it they had two outboard motors, a five horsepower and a ten horsepower, one serving as a spare. The survival equipment issued by the department included a fish net and a rifle.
The search was started when Mackenzie Air Services, which were to keep check on the party and resupply it if necessary, failed to make contact on two scheduled rendezvous. The upturned canoe used by the girls was found floating on the northwest shore of Good Hope bay, on Great Bear lake, on July

Inquiries oj the Ministry 19. The search is being continued by air and by ground by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Departmental officials point out the possibility, from information available to them, that the canoe may have drifted away while the girls were working on the shore of the lake, and for this reason all hope is not abandoned.
Miss Kroeger was born in Hamburg, Germany. She was experienced in bush travel, having worked on the same project for the Arctic institute in 1958. Miss Goodfellow is a native of Plaster Rock, New Brunswick.
In answer to the supplementary question, I must say that it is not the practice of the department to encourage women to undertake field work, particularly in remote areas. However, women scientists of proven technical or professional qualifications, for example geologists or geographers, are occasionally assigned to field operations when physically fit to undertake such tasks. The two missing girls are the only female scientists on field parties of our department in remote areas.
Whether it be for male or female employees, the department makes every possible effort to ensure the safety of its field officers while in the bush. The precautionary measures include prearranged contacts by commercial air services, radio communications where possible, outfitting the parties with extra accessories such as outboard motors, training in first aid and the provision of a means for living off the land from game and fish if temporarily stranded. With an average of nearly 2,000 employees in our field operations each summer, including our hydrographic operations, there is always a risk of some casualties.
Mr. Speaker, in addressing myself to the families of the two missing girls I wish to say how much we share their anxiety and their sorrow. I should like to assure them that all that is possible is being done to find the missing girls if, perchance, they are still alive.

I thank the minister for the answer. I would hope that it might be possible to continue Mr. Hay in this position if he desires it. I say that for two main reasons. One is that I think he is very well qualified for the position, and the other is the importance to the country of having the vast experience of Mr. Hay available to the commission. The commission is largely comprised now of new members with very little background of experience in this particular activity, and-and I say this with deference to them, and I hope this remark will not be misunderstood-with little detailed knowledge of the history of the work done by this commission and its predecessors in office. I would therefore hope that the continuity of historical knowledge and experience, in a detailed and practical way, of the activities of the commission and its predecessors would be retained for the benefit of this commission and the government.
I have always taken a great interest in the important work of this commission in developing the national capital area in relation to the whole of the country. I think that view has been shared by all prime ministers since the scheme was first started in the 1890's, or perhaps I shoud say the scheme and its predecessors. I believe all prime ministers in the intervening years have attached that importance to it.
I want to raise one matter of some criticism of the minister. It is meant more in the nature of a critical warning than in any other way. This commission was always answerable to the prime minister of the country and in that way was removed from the vicissitudes, shall I say, of party warfare, because of the high interest of the current prime minister in those activities.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: And the present Prime Minister will continue to do so, undoubtedly.

Perhaps the hon. member for Carleton will just bear with me for a moment until I make the point. That may be the answer to the point and it may not be the answer; I do not know. However, I want to deal with this subject matter. That has been the history of this commission over the years. It has been kept remarkably free from the vicissitudes of party warfare. I think all hon. members will agree that has been the fact, and that has been in general the concept in approaching this commission and problems relating to it.
The minister made answerable in the House of Commons for the activities of the commission is now the Minister of Public Works. I think the examination of the estimates of that department over the last few days of this session and over every session as far as the records go back since confederation will indicate that this department has been notorious for the fact that it has not been removed from the vicissitudes of party warfare. I find a real danger in the fact that this commission has been made answerable to the Minister of Public Works, the danger being that it may in the course of time be brought into the area of the ordinary activities of the Minister of Public Works.
I hope that will not be the case. I am not in any way referring to the competence of the present Minister of Public Works in relation to his duties with respect to the commission, nor to that of any preceding or succeeding minister in that respect. I for one rather regret that the commission was assigned to the Minister of Public Works and is to be answerable to him from time to time. That remark, as the minister will appreciate, refers to the continuing office of minister as opposed to anything having to do with the person holding that office at any given time. But there is a danger there which I think the committee should be aware of, and I hope the government, including the Minister of Public Works, will bear that in mind.
That brings me directly to the point which I think should be mentioned at this time. It concerns the method of hiring casual labour in the year 1960. A practice was used in the method of hiring this year which was, to say the least, very shocking to anyone who had followed the activities of this commission over the years. Whether or not it was caused by certain employees acting without authority I do not know, but there was an apparent requirement that anyone applying for work when the summer employees were being taken on had to produce a letter

either from certain members of parliament or from certain political associations which had worked on behalf of the present government before they could be interviewed for employment. I am quite sure that is not the wish of any member of this House of Commons, and I say without fear of contradiction that that has certainly never been the approach to this problem over the last several decades.
When this matter arose I immediately drew it to the attention of the Minister of Public Works. He disclaimed all knowledge of it but said he would look into it, and that if this practice did exist and was being carried on it would be immediately stopped. I must out of fairness say that he was very quick to take that stand and to make his position quite clear and unequivocal.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. member a question? The hon. member for Ottawa West did mention that to me some months ago and I asked him if there was any proof of any kind which he could give me, but he did not have any proof except that someone had told him. I investigated through Mr. Hay and other sources and found that there was absolutely no truth whatever in such an allegation.
However, we do give preference to married men, and it is an amazing thing in many jobs how the casual labour do bring in letters from all sorts of people, including letters from the hon. member for Ottawa West. That is perfectly natural. The casual labourer who is not well known needs to have some indication of his bona fides and he should go to his member of parliament, whoever he may be, whether the hon. member for Ottawa West or somebody else. But we have so many applicants for casual labour jobs that we are able to employ only a few of them; but I can assure the hon. member that neither the Prime Minister nor myself would ever want the national capital commission to be a subject of party politics, and I am very distressed to think that the hon. member would even suggest that it might be. There is no reason whatever for making such a statement, and we are very proud of the national capital commission.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The hon. minister asked if he could ask a question. The hon. member for Ottawa West has the floor.

The minister in his eagerness to give an answer rose on the excuse of asking a question, and I made way for him. If the minister had just forborne a little I think he would have been in a little better position to make an effective answer when he asked his question. His question took

a curious form for one so experienced and so very capable in asking questions.
The point I was making was that I immediately drew the matter to the attention of the minister, and I think I accurately stated the position he took; that he had no knowledge of it whatever but he would look into it immediately and if there was any such practice he would correct it at once. The summer hiring of labour terminated at about that point, and I have had no further complaint since that time.
However, the minister went a bit further in his so-called question and made certain allegations about letters from me. I brought the two letters I wrote, and I am quite prepared to place them on record if the committee wants them, but they involve names of individuals who are perfectly innocent and I ask the committee to consider that fact.
The point in regard to the letters turns on this, that there was a practice at that time requiring a man to have a letter from a member before he was able to obtain employment from the commission, and I will be happy to give the minister the letters. The other letter says that the man in question had been advised by one of the employees of the commission that if he had a letter from a member he could obtain employment with the commission. That will be seen quite clearly if the minister reads these letters, so the minister was put on the spot as to whether this was a new practice or not.
My complaint here is in the nature of a warning to the minister, if I may use that term, not to let this practice creep into the national capital commission. If, as I suspect, it was being done by some overzealous new employees on their own authority, it should be checked into, and if corrective action is required it should be taken; because I think the minister will readily agree that it is an approach that is highly undesirable. I am quite sure that if he looks up the record he will find where the present Prime Minister took that view on a previous occasion when discussing matters of the commission.

I keep the Prime Minister in touch with everything we do. He has an enormous variety of tasks, but I try to keep him posted and give him an outline of what we are doing.

I had better tell the minister what the facts of life are if he persists in the practice of interrupting improperly in the course of debate when a matter is being raised, I think perfectly fairly.
It is a matter of opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I will not interrupt again, but you do not mind my saying that, do you?

The minister is taking the offensive in a case like this; it is a very good court tactic, but he knows that if I disclose the names of these men who were able to get the letters they would be hounded by other employees, and he and others responsible for the national capital commission would never find out about it or know why those men had been fired.
Let the minister not go on with that nonsense. He will recall that I told him earlier that I feared there would be rioting while these applications were being considered. On two or three mornings while these letters were being demanded before prospective employees were admitted for interviews the situation was very rough indeed. Fortunately the practice does not seem to have been continued, because I have not received any further complaints. But the situation was very rough, and if the minister thinks I am going to disclose the names of employees who were fortunate enough to take the necessary measures and get interviews in order to be taken on, he has another thought coming. He surely knows, from his administrative experience, that employees at a junior level have ways of spiking other employees and obtaining their dismissal without senior officials in the commission knowing anything about it.
If the minister will read my remarks carefully he will see I was very careful not to attribute blame to him in regard to this matter and I was careful, also, not to attribute blame to the commission itself or to the senior employees of the commision. That is exactly the situation. I place the matter on record so that the minister may be forewarned and able to deal with it again if it arises.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my views and opinions on national capital planning have been expressed publicly with such frequency and regularity that their reiteration now is perhaps a work of supererogation. Therefore I shall detain the committee only very briefly.
The past year has been notable for two of the most significant achievements of all time in national capital planning. The first was that at long last the plan of railway relocation has been adopted by the national capital commission and the government. Within a short time I hope the first steps will have been taken in this project which spells such a significant advance for the national capital. Second, I call attention to the fact that the green belt purchases have now reached more than the halfway mark. This great national project has involved many growing pains; there are still serious problems of valuation to be settled, but its impact will be profound for generations.
One of the immediate results of the green belt development may already be seen in the fine new campus-type industrial development of the Northern Electric Company now taking shape at Crystal bay. My hope is that the green belt acquisitions may be completed in the near future on a basis fair and equitable to the individual land owners and to the government of Canada.
This word of caution I utter. It is vital, in my view, that the development outside the green belt be a planned development, a zoned development, concentrated into self-contained hamlets and not merely an ugly un-coordinated suburban sprawl which has simply leapfrogged the green belt. The national capital commission should attach the highest priority to assistance to the area municipalities in the development of proper satellite communities on the perimeter of the green belt.
What of the future? Effective and adequate liaison between the national capital commission and the area municipalities must be achieved. There is no real problem here, but I venture to submit to the present chairman, in whose competence and good judgment I have the most complete confidence, that he can make in this field the greatest contribution of his already distinguished career. Effective collaboration, strengthened co-operation between national capital commission and the area municipalities; I believe those should be the watchwords of the Minister of Public Works and the watchwords of Mr. Alan K. Hay during his term as chairman of the commission.
Among the new projects to be undertaken, I believe the Ottawa river parkway takes highest priority. Properly designed, it will be


an almost revolutionary addition to our parkway system. To the whole capital it will give new character, added personality and distinction. No other project can have such immediate significance.
The year 1967, the centennial year of confederation, ought to be establishsed now as the target date for the completion of the present phases of the national capital plan. Completion of the physical aspects of the plan during the next seven years will enable the central celebration of our hundredth anniversary to be in a capital which has achieved a cultural, intellectual and spiritual maturity as well as physical beauty and geographic unity.
This city has certain basic physical requirements if it is to achieve the cultural purposes, the national purposes, which ought to be the objectives of a capital city. May I mention three which we alone of the great capitals, lack. First, we need a large and impressive conference or assembly hall in which great events of national and international importance might take place; second, a national theatre and music hall in which a national festival of the arts could be held which might attract the outstanding theatrical, musical, artistic and cultural events of the day; and third, we need a large sports stadium and arena.
We have just seven years before the centennial of confederation to achieve these essential attributes of a national capital. Not for a moment do I suggest that these projects are the sole responsibility of the federal government. They must be achieved through effective collaboration, and in that I hope and believe that my old friend, the Minister of Public Works, will give effective and dynamic leadership.
This I emphasize, that the time to plan and prepare these projects is now. Only if we have them by 1967 can we have what one of our most mature and articulate journalists- Mr. I. Norman Smith of the Ottawa Journal- described as "a mature capital, a live capital, an exciting capital, that stirs patriotism and pride" or, to use another phrase of his in the same distinguished front page editorial one filled "with vision, beauty, learning, the arts, the nation's character".
One further matter. A number of the most basic and far-reaching advances in national capital planning have been achieved under the guidance of the present Prime Minister. The right hon. gentleman developed a profound interest in this community, an imaginative concept of its future similar to the interest of three of his great predecessors, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Sir Robert Borden and Mr. W. L. Mackenzie King, the three earlier prime ministers who were the principal

architects of the national capital. While I know the Prime Minister's deep interest will continue, I would like on behalf of the national capital area to express warm appreciation of his vital accomplishments during the time he was the minister responsible for the national capital commission. He has blazed an exciting trail for my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, whose accomplishments in the next 12 months the committee will confidently anticipate.

Mr. Chairman, I will not speak as eloquently as the hon. member for Carleton, though my feelings as to the deeds of those who created the federal district commission and the national capital commission are just as profound. I believe that	history	will reveal	that	theGreber plan	was a	great vision,	one	that
has been brought forward and accomplished in part. To that extent I suppose the present Prime Minister will have a part in that vision.
I am not rising to criticize any feature of the national	capital	commission.	On	thecontrary, I and the citizens of Ottawa appreciate the	work	accomplished	by	the
federal district commission and the national capital commission. One of my criticisms is not even directed to the work of the national capital commission, but rather to the failure of the federal government to do anything with respect to the Expropriation Act. I am not going to reiterate the story, because I have frequently outlined it in this chamber since 1945. I expected that after the throne speech debate this year we would have had an opportunity to examine a new Expropriation Act, but this has not developed.
I am not complaining of the fact that the recent judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada relieved the national capital commission and the government with respect to those lands which have already been expropriated. Any other ruling would have created vast confusion. However, I do ask the minister in his capacity as Minister of Public Works as well as spokesman for the national capital commission to take a deep interest in bringing in amendments to the Expropriation Act. I say we need a new act. I suspect that anything that might have been brought before us at this session would have been useless in the light of present day thinking, in the year 1960, with respect to the expropriation of land by the government.
The provincial government of Ontario has established a committee to investigate land expropriation. Some time ago I advised the Minister of Justice about this and asked him 79951-0-4251
Supply-Public Works
to have his officials attend those meetings to gather information and learn the opinions of those appearing before committee, with a view to bringing in a better expropriation act. It is absolutely unfair to operate under an act that is almost 100 years old and which gives the government power to impinge on civil rights. Surely in this so-called free world in 1960 civil rights should be properly protected under the Expropriation Act. Civil rights are not a matter that should be lightly touched upon by a federal government, because they involve provincial jurisdiction. The late premier of the province of Quebec did not hesitate to say so, and I agree with him in that respect. In the past the taking over of land for the purposes of roads and parks in connection with the federal district commission was outside the powers of this parliament and beyond its jurisdiction without some agreement being made with the provincial governments concerned.
Before the time of the present minister, governments in the past went lightly about expropriating land on this side of the river, but acted a little more cautiously on the other side of the river. In this God-fearing, law-abiding province on this side of the river the government expropriated everything it wanted. As a result we had two approaches in relation to expropriation. On the other side of the river a piece of land brought the price it should have commanded, and on this side it brought whatever the government offered for it. This condition cannot continue. The courts cannot do anything about it. They do not lean toward the government, but they must operate under the act as it stands. In its present form the act does not provide for fair value to the owner and does not take into consideration all the factors that should be considered when land and property rights are taken from an individual for other than essential services of the government.
I have always accepted the old theory of expropriation, that the government should be permitted to take land for essential government works such as a railway, a post office, a defence establishment, a building for national revenue, etc. When it comes to giving the same power of expropriation to crown corporations or as in this case to the federal district commission and later the national capital commission I take a different attitude. The Expropriation Act should be amended to allow more generous promises in estimating the value of the land.
There is much to be said about the matter of expropriation under the National Capital Act. I believe I am right in saying that any land expropriated may be sold. I understand

Supply-Public Works this will happen in time; the land which has been bought will be resold in the future. Understandably it is being leased now in accordance with the powers given to the federal district commission. A profit will be made at a future time when the land is resold. The land was not required for the purpose for which it was expropriated in the first place. That is a good reason why in such cases the act should make it possible for fairer treatment to be given to the party whose land is expropriated. Without going into further detail the minister will understand this problem which is of concern to the citizens of Ottawa and surrounding area.
Again I urge the minister to request his colleague the Minister of Justice, to send his officials to observe the proceedings of the Ontario government's land expropriation committee, which is doing an excellent job. If this were done, and particularly if the Minister of Public Works were also to send his officials to that committee, he would be in a position to assist the Minister of Justice and perhaps make him more aware of the problems that the Minister of Public Works will face in the near future when confronted with further expropriations.
With respect to Ottawa East, I urge the minister to do something about improving Sussex drive, which should be selected as the site of important public buildings. There is no point in neglecting this attractive area on which so much money has been spent, nor is there any point in making additional improvements if we leave a few decrepit old brick residences and shabby temporary buildings like those which house the income tax offices to mar its beauty.
Some years ago it was proposed that the national museum or perhaps a building for the Department of External Affairs would be erected on the south side of Sussex drive facing the river. There is no more beautiful site in Ottawa. I spoke to the minister about this some time ago. I am hoping he will take action in this regard. Surely he and the officials of his department have as keen eyes as do the local residents, tourists and others who pass by. If it were not for the French embassy and Earnscliffe there would be no building of beauty there. It is one of the finest locations in the city. It has Rideau falls and is a fine scenic drive. I hope that some time in the future there will also be an interprovincial bridge there. This is a beautiful site for some substantial government buildings.
I have another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. It has to do with King Edward avenue, which was at one time a beautiful avenue. It has a centre boulevard with trees and lawns. I was

surprised to be told some years ago in the committee which dealt with the federal district commission that the commission had no interest in this avenue and no responsibility for it. Could it not co-operate with the city of Ottawa, which I am sure would be glad to do so, and take over this avenue and beautify it? It is the avenue which leads from Sussex drive, from the Governor General's residence and from the two bridges over the Rideau river. The federal district commission should take an interest in King Edward avenue. If it does not, this avenue will be turned into a commercial street.
These are the two matters that I wished to bring to the attention of the minister at this time. I could mention many others, but I hope the minister will take a second look at these two matters in the constituency of Ottawa East, and when he visits his good friend the Prime Minister or the Governor General, not simply proceed down Sussex drive with his eyes looking straight ahead but look around and see whether he can do something about this, and whether he should have some great public buildings placed on this most beautiful site.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks on this item will be few. Of course my appreciation of the structure and functions of the national capital commission, formerly the federal district commission, is not so extensive as that of the hon. member for Carleton or the two hon. members from Ottawa who have been in the house for several years representing this area.
I say without hesitation that there are some beautiful parks in Ottawa. I understand that the national capital commission or its predecessor had quite a bit to do in developing such places as the driveway, but as one who does not come from Ottawa I say there are some parts of the city that I am extremely disappointed with. I do not think they add flavour to the capital of Canada.
I have noticed that we have at the moment an excellent capital city in a glass case on Sparks street. I believe this is what Ottawa is supposed to look like some years hence. There are some parts of the city itself that I think many visitors to Ottawa are disappointed with, and I refer to tourists particularly and those who come from other parts of the country and are here for short periods of time on some sort of business.
During the springtime particularly the thing which really irks me is to see this annual patchwork program that is carried out on some of the streets or roads of Ottawa. I do not know whether this comes under the national capital commission or whether the

hon. member for Russell has anything to do with the building and maintenance of the roads. I may say, Mr. Chairman, that in the interior part of my constituency in northern British Columbia we have quite an experience with potholes in the spring, when the frost is coming out of the ground and frost boils are developing. Consequently our deep holes in the road are nothing but bottomless pits of mud. Yet we do not go quite to the extent that they go to here, namely running annual contests as to who can find the largest pothole in the city. It seems sort of odd that a city which has been in existence for so many years should have such difficulties with its streets every spring. This is certainly something that does not endear the city to visitors when they see this sort of thing going on. A fair amount of effort should be exerted to get this question cleared up.
As I said, I do not know whether my hon. friend from Russell has any jurisdiction over this or whether it comes within the field of the national capital commission. I understand that this commission in developing the national capital is working more along the lines of a co-operative venture among the three levels of government rather than one level of government having the entire jurisdiction.
I suggest that many years ago we should have started on an extensive program of slum clearance in areas which are not too far from this very building. In this area housing conditions are not good. On occasions other hon. members besides myself, who do not come from Ottawa or live here for any extended time, have spoken on this matter. They have gained their knowledge after having travelled extensively within the city limits.
There seems to be an inordinately high number of decrepit buildings or fire traps or slum areas that should be eliminated, not only for the sake of beautifying the city but for the sake of providing a decent environment for the people who have to live in those particular areas. There is much to do that has not yet been done. I am not being critical of what was done before, but I am sure the federal district commission, the national capital commission, the city of Ottawa and the Ontario government have concerned themselves with some areas, and excellent strides have been made in beautifying the city in an endeavour to approach the reality that exists in the glass case down on Sparks street.
Yet there appears to be so much to do, and surely we could engage in an extensive crash program not only on roads, which is only one item, but on slum clearance, the elimination
Supply-Public Works of fire traps and the development of all other fields that need to be developed in order that this may become a beautiful capital city.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I wish to congratulate the Minister of Public Works on the chairman he has selected for this commission. I am sorry that the appointment is only a temporary one, because I doubt whether there is another man in Canada who has the qualifications necessary for doing the job that has to be done, if he were given sufficient time.
I listened with a great deal of attention to the well prepared speech of the hon. member for Carleton, who submitted many suggestions to the national capital commission which would be not only profitable to the city of Ottawa but are necessary for the capital of the nation. I can say that I agree with him most thoroughly. The only thing I do not agree with is the suggestion he made that part of these things which are for the benefit of the nation should be paid for by some of the municipalities, who are going to benefit by reason of having the buildings within their boundaries. I am sure my hon. friend knows that the municipality of Ottawa and the adjoining municipalities are suffering enough now from the contributions they are making toward a national capital. They should not be called upon to contribute any more money toward buildings which are going to be for the benefit of all Canadians. I am sure it would be easy enough to convince my hon. friend from Carleton if we were to have a short conversation and I were to show him the figures of the contributions made by more than one municipality, but particularly the city of Ottawa.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman misinterpreted what I said.

Perhaps I did, and if that is so I think that is all the more reason why we should have the conference I suggested. I would not want the hon. member for Carleton to lead the Canadian people to believe that the provision of such buildings as he proposes, and which are necessary for a national capital, should not be the responsibility of the people of Canada as a whole rather than the responsibility of the citizens of Ottawa.
Actually, it is time the program to establish the national capital was accelerated. I am not saying this in any way as criticism of the present administration or the national capital commission, but rather as a means of encouraging the minister to realize that the national capital is actually a Canadian city for the benefit of all Canadians. The program for the erection of these buildings that will be necessary should be accelerated so that.

Supply-Public Works as my hon. friend suggested, during our centennial celebration in 1967 we will have a capital city of which all Canadians can be proud. I know the Minister of Public Works will make his contribution toward making this possible.
There are several things that should be attended to by the national capital commission. As the result of conversations I have had with members of the commission, I think there is a possibility of reaching agreement on the national capital commission making some contribution toward the extension of services through land owned by the commission, where the land on both sides of the capital commission land is fully developed. I am of the opinion that since the national capital commission create the problem, they should be responsible for the extension of the services through the land they own. As a result of their failure to do this they are putting an additional burden on the taxpayers of the city of Ottawa.
Let me say at once that the city of Ottawa is treated considerably better now so far as grants in lieu of taxes are concerned than it has been for some years. For a number of years the city of Ottawa was neglected in this respect and the citizens made a more than reasonable contribution toward the establishment of the national capital. It is not too late for the Department of Public Works to make recommendations to remedy this situation, providing that the number of years during which the city of Ottawa paid for the development of the national capital should be taken into consideration. One manner in which this could be accomplished would' be for the Department of Public Works to accept the charges for local improvements extended through land owned by the national capital commission where the adjacent land is fully developed.
There is another small problem to which I should like to refer, and that is the price paid for land expropriated in the green belt. I think all the citizens of Ottawa and the surrounding area agree that a green belt is necessary if we are to have a properly planned capital city. I presume that the price paid for land expropriated by the national capital commission for the green belt is set by the commission's valuators. However, in my opinion the price is too low when compared with the price paid for land adjacent to the green belt which has been sold to private individuals.
I believe also that whatever land is going to be purchased for the green belt should be purchased immediately. I do not believe the people who are to have their property expropriated should be kept waiting longer than is reasonable after expropriation to have a

settlement made. Many people who are living in the green belt, and whose property is to be expropriated, intend to relocate somewhere else. Some system should be established whereby the process of expropriation could be speeded up, thus avoiding injustice to these people and enabling them to relocate as soon as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Is he aware that 98 per cent of the property taken over for the green belt has been purchased as the result of friendly agreement, and only 2 per cent by expropriation? I was wondering what his suggestion was.
I know it has been done in that manner. I did not know what the percentage was, but I am glad to hear the minister say that it was 98 per cent. I have no reason to doubt that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: We thought the hon. member might ask the question, so we looked up the answer in advance.

Actually, many people in the green belt suffer from the fear that their property is going to be expropriated. They fear that they are going to be kept waiting a year or two afterwards before a settlement is arrived at. I agree that many of these fears are based on rumours, but it would be better if settlements could be arrived at without expropriation. I know that neither the minister nor the national capital commission would want these people to suffer any injustice.
I was rather sorry to hear that the hon. member for Skeena does not like the city of Ottawa. Perhaps his dislike results from the fact that he has been here longer than he expected to be.
Not as long as I expect to be.

I meant longer this session than he expected to be. This makes it easier for him to see the things that are wrong with the city of Ottawa. Like all cities we have a patching program for the roads, but that is not the responsibility of the government or the national capital commission; it is the responsibility of the city of Ottawa. The reason the patching is not done as efficiently or as speedily as the hon. member would like is the same reason I mentioned earlier, that the dominion government has not at any time accepted responsibility for paying its full share of the cost of city services. This condition has existed for a long time and is not entirely the responsibility of this government, because it also existed under previous governments.

Even today the dominion government does not make payment on the basis of the city of Ottawa assessment but rather on the basis of the dominion government's assessment, and the result is that the grant in lieu of taxes is made on a lower basis than that upon which private residents or commercial users pay for these services.
There is another reason for the condition of the roads in the city of Ottawa. The weather here is much more severe than in British Columbia, and the resultant damage to the roads is much greater. I have not been in British Columbia for a long time, but when I was there I was not greatly impressed by the condition of the roads. However, I did not make any remarks publicly about that matter because I realized that whenever there is work to be done there is a financial problem connected with it. We in the Liberal party realize that the financial question sometimes becomes a very important part of the problem to be solved.
You are comparing two different things.

This is not done for the purpose of creating confusion. I have been comparing the roads in British Columbia and the roads in Ottawa. I am not comparing two different things; I am comparing two different roads in connection with the same problem.
Then I noted that the hon. member said he felt badly about the radio and press competition that took place in connection with the pothole situation in Ottawa. This competition probably resulted from the fact that during January, February and March the dominion government did not do much, so there was a lack of news. The news media want to create news, and the first thing they noticed was the potholes. Actually if the hon. member for Skeena and my hon. friend had been more active at that time I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that there would have been a great deal more news and they would not have noticed the potholes in the city of Ottawa.
There has been some criticism about some parts of Ottawa having poor housing. It is no excuse for the city of Ottawa, but I think other cities have the same problem and that the solution to it is urban renewal. Urban renewal is considerably complicated, because people who own houses that should be demolished in any section that should be due for urban renewal put a great deal of value on their houses, thus creating a great deal of cost and making the problem more difficult to solve. As to our present program, with the preparations the capital city is making in favour of urban renewal, I am
Supply-Public Works sure it will not be too long before some real progress is made and is apparent.
It was also suggested that the city of Ottawa, with the help of the dominion government if they would take their full responsibility for the tax roll, could have a crash program. At present, however when the city of Ottawa draws its taxes from real estate only and the contribution from the present government is not sufficient to pay for the services which are extended by the city of Ottawa, crash programs for financial reasons are impossible.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a suggestion to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker).
First, I should like to commend the government, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) and the Minister of Public Works for always taking great interest in the development of the national capital. I would also ask the Minister of Public Works to consider setting up an advisory town planning committee, composed of town planners from across Canada, with members from every province and perhaps also from the large metropolitan centres. There now exists in Canada an institute of professional town planners, and in almost every province there is a professional town planners' society. The proposed committee could help the national capital commission work out a general policy designed to give the national capital a distinctive Canadian character reflecting the unity of the Canadian nation in its diverse aspects. In that way, the committee might help promote what some of my colleagues have called for, namely that special distinctive character which would be a characteristic and lasting feature of the national capital.
Thus, with the co-operation of town planners across Canada, the development of the national capital could become a common endeavour shared in by the best town planning authorities in Canada. We could thus achieve the purpose we all have in mind, making our national capital one of the most beautiful cities in the world.

Mr. Chairman, I should like, first of all, to commend the Minister of Public Works very sincerely for his excellent choice

Supply-Public Works in appointing Mr. Hay as chairman of the national capital commission. I know there is no man more interested in the planning of the capital nor more able to take care of that significant task. I hope that the government will have the wisdom to keep him a long time as head of the national capital commission.
I would also ask the minister to see to the continued development of Gatineau park. The house knows surely that Gatineau park is part of the national capital planning, and also that it is the only national park in the province of Quebec. The commission has already done a great deal of work in this park and, quite recently, or rather last fall, a section of road connecting Gatineau park with Gamelin boulevard was opened to the public. People can now travel a distance of some 15 miles from Hull to the centre of Gatineau park. I suggest to hon. members, while they are here in Ottawa, to take a drive on that road and see the work that has been done in that area of my riding.
I would also ask the minister to approach the provincial government for the settlement of two problems, one of which has to do with land that belongs to the province of Quebec and is part of Gatineau park. I know that attempts were made in the past by the commission to settle the matter with the former provincial government but no agreement was reached. But on the other hand, as there has been a change of government, it should now be possible to settle the problem. In addition, I should like to ask the minister to try and solve the problem of a second road between Hull and the town of Aylmer.
At the present time, the commission has title to the right of way which used to belong to the Hull Electric Company, of Hull and Aylmer. Now, because of extremely heavy traffic on Aylmer road, a second road between Hull and Aylmer has become a necessity. I therefore ask the minister to take this up with the Quebec minister of highways, so that some agreement might be reached with regard to those two projects.
I would also ask the minister to follow up the town of Aylmer's request for a public beach at Aylmer, on the Ottawa river.
I am very happy to note the progress made in the national capital development.
The progress made on certain important projects is indeed remarkable. Furthermore, I am very glad that the commission had decided to relocate the railways. That, I believe, is the key to the whole development


project in the national capital and I know that, four or five years from now, when the tracks will have been removed from the city of Ottawa, when the station will occupy a new site, it will transform the downtown area of the national capital.
I am convinced that the commission is doing excellent work and I urge it to keep it up so that, by the time we celebrate the centennial of confederation, we will have a capital worthy of the magnificent country which is Canada.

There are two points I want to raise. While they may trench on other items, since they relate to general policy perhaps they could best be raised on this first item. One has to do with acquisition of land in the green belt, and I think in this good progress is being made by the commission. But the point is this, that the policy has been to acquire land in the green belt by negotiation. I have no quarrel with that; however, the situation is now developing that certain owners in the green belt, because of the amount of time which has elapsed since the announcement that the green belt was being taken over by the government, have had some family circumstance occur, as for instance the death of the one operating the property, the husband in most cases, and have found themselves unable to continue their ordinary activity with their land. For all practical purposes, although there are no legal restrictions against it, they cannot borrow money on mortgage, and if they do borrow money on mortgage the rate of interest is 7 per cent.
These people are left in an awkward position where they cannot effectively deal with their land because of the announcement that it is being taken over by the government for green belt purposes, but they have not the rights acquired by one whose land is being expropriated; and indeed those remedies are not quite satisfactory to meet their problem. There is in a few cases very real hardship created by reason of the awkward position in which these people find themselves. They are neither persons whose property has been expropriated nor persons who are free to deal with their land as they see fit.
I draw this matter to the attention of the minister because in those cases it is not possible under the law, while negotiations are pending, for the commission to make an advance to them by way of compensation. I think he will agree that the commission does not have such a right under the law. I point

this out to the minister so he will be aware of it and will try to see that whatever action can be taken within the law is taken to meet those very few but very difficult situations.
The second point I want to raise has to do with another matter, and perhaps if I ask the minister a simple question it would elucidate the problem. Under item 315, covering interest charges on outstanding loans made for the purpose of acquiring property in the national capital region, could the minister indicate what rate of interest is paid to the finance department for the advances made?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Five and three quarters per cent.

When expropriation proceedings are taken or a settlement is arrived at with the commission, there is provision in the option agreement whereby, if there is a delay beyond a reasonable time which is not due to any action on the part of the person whose property is being taken over, interest will be paid by the commission at the rate of 5 per cent per annum.
In the great majority of cases the settlement is completed well within the time indicated, and indeed in recent months the minister has done some very effective work in speeding up completion of the transactions and payment after settlement is made. But in these few cases where for some reason or other there is delay in obtaining approval from the government or where there is unusual delay for some other reason, the crown pays less interest to the person whose property is expropriated than the commission itself is charged by the finance department, and indeed much less than the person whose property is being taken over has to pay.
In a few cases that can work quite severe hardship, as the minister will readily appreciate, and I ask him to give his views to the committee and to seek to have that situation remedied so that the interest rate paid by the national capital commission in those cases where there is unreasonable delay, not due to any fault of the person whose property is being taken, is raised in keeping with the current rate on borrowed money.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I would like to add my support to the fine speech by the hon. member for Carleton on our national capital. Ottawa, as everyone knows, belongs to our whole country and people even as far away as Athabasca take a great interest in its future.
I also want to speak about parking because I have an intimate knowledge of this problem, having directed parking on this hill back in 1947 and I have not seen very much 79951-0-426
Supply-Public Works improvement since. We have an excellent spot down on the river bank where we could park thousands of automobiles if we had the proper accommodation. Another reason why I think this is a good place for parking is that it would require very little rock excavation which, as you know, is very expensive on the hill. The cost of some of our government buildings has gone well beyond the original appropriation because of the rock cuts. Down along the river bank we could build these spiral ramps down into a big parking lot, and the original cost would not be excessive because if properly planned it could be built in sections. You could provide facilities for 1,500 cars in the first plan and then expand it to perhaps 3,000 or 4,000 cars.
This need not interfere with the beauty of the site, as several hon. members have mentioned, because it could be blended with the natural beauty of the river bank; and I think in any plans for Ottawa the beauty of our capital is something we should all bear in mind. I should like to see something done about this well before 1967.
I would also like to back the idea of a proper theatre or assembly hall. In Alberta they built two such buildings which have added greatly to the cultural and civic life of that province, and I am sure our nation can afford buildings of the same beauty and magnitude. I think it is appropriate to go on with them at this time when unemployment is still one of our serious problems, and to go ahead with the beautification of Ottawa is something which I am sure hon. members from all over Canada would heartily approve.

Mr. Chairman, I think we have done considerable in relation to parkways and improvements on national capital commission land, but I am surprised that consideration has not been given to some relationship between the city of Ottawa and the commission to try to eliminate, when we clear the slums of Ottawa, industrial development in the city proper. This is a considerable distance from the other buildings which were built years ago, such as the supreme court building and the Confederation building, and as we continue to push outward from the centre of the capital we should take into consideration where the industrial part of Ottawa is going to be, if there is going to be one.
In determining the location of industrial sites we should take into account the experience of Washington, D.C., the capital city of

I think the commission should work, in co-operation with the city of Ottawa itself, toward the development of a national capital that will be as free as possible of industrial development. speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. Brooks (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speechtext:
May I say at the outset that after waiting a long, long time, I am very pleased to get my estimates before the committee. Last year when the estimates of my department were submitted to this committee I gave a rather comprehensive review of the work of the department and of the Canadian pension commission. I do not think I need again re-examine the background of the veterans legislation and show the progress made over the years. I propose to confine my present remarks to a brief review of what has happened during the fiscal year just ended and to provide some general information on a number of items in these estimates.
My department has enjoyed a satisfactory year of accomplishment and looks forward to further progress during the current year in the care of our veteran population. Although 15 years have now passed since the conclusion of hostilities in world war II and over 40 years have elapsed since world war I was brought to a successful termination, the many veterans who participated in these and earlier struggles and in the action in Korea still have many disabilities and problems which are properly referred to my department. We have found, indeed, that many of the difficulties which veterans are now experiencing require continuing, skilled attention.
As hon. members know, the main estimates of the department, the Canadian pension commission and the war veterans allowance board, which are now before you, were referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs. They were thoroughly reviewed by that committee and have been

subject to close scrutiny and questioning by its members, who have shown creditable knowledge of our affairs. I wish to express my thanks to the standing committee for the interest they took during their detailed study. I wish particularly to express my appreciation to the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton who performed unusually well the exacting duties of chairman.
The veterans welfare services have continued to provide much assistance in the welfare field, including counselling, but their major contribution is the assistance they give in the processing and implementation of awards made under the War Veterans Allowance Act, the assistance fund, W.V.A., and the regulations. The facilities of the veterans welfare services branch meet increasing demands due to the progressive impairment of the capacities of veterans because of the ageing process, particularly as it applies to world war I veterans.
The Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act continues in its scope to exceed our original expectations. The number of children approved for assistance under the act from its inception in 1953 to March 31, 1959 was 1,406. During the last fiscal year there were 362 new children approved. The number actively pursuing courses of education as of March 31 of this year was 858. Many of the students assisted under this act have told us that this opportunity enabled them to complete a university education which would otherwise have been impossible.
The Returned Soldiers Insurance Act and the Veterans Insurance Act now provide a combined total of $114 million in life insurance protection. These measures have enabled many veterans and widows to provide for themselves an estate which otherwise would not have been possible through life insurance because of disabilities which rendered them uninsurable commercially. Eligibility to contract for veterans insurance was reopened in 1958, and I am pleased to say that in the fiscal year 1959-60 there were 2,320 new policies issued for a total face amount of $8,558,000, making a total of 4,528 policies with a face value of about $16 million which have been issued since the act was amended.
The remaining re-establishment credits available under the provisions of the War Service Grants Act are being made available in increasing amounts as the remaining period during which they will be available becomes shorter. We estimate that this statutory item will, during the present year, amount to some $2,500,000. Active efforts are being pursued in order to ensure that all veterans with outstanding credits are approached in order that they may make the

most satisfactory use of their remaining credits. A study is being made of the trends noticed in the administration of our welfare services with a view to future planning, in order that the intended welfare functions may be adequately maintained and foreseen.
I now come to the treatment services provided by the department. All hon. members are aware that the institutions operated by this branch of the department are held in high regard, and their reputation for providing first class treatment is being well maintained. The doctors and nursing staff continue to provide professional service of a high order. We are particularly appreciative of those doctors on whom the department calls on a part time basis. These consultants deserve our warmest thanks. We continue to have difficulty in finding adequate numbers of trained nursing staff. However, the problem, which is not confined to the department, was relieved somewhat for us by the salary increases granted to nurses some eight months ago.

This is the height of the dinner hour. The administrative cost of running our hospitals will increase somewhat this year over the actual expenditure we made in the year 1959-60, increasing from about $55,900,000 to some $57,367,000. Of that total cost, however, we expect to recover some $12,730,000. These recoveries are increasing, due largely to payments from the provinces for treatment given to patients having entitlement under provincial hospital insurance plans.
I should mention that our hospital construction program is proceeding satisfactorily. The replacement of obsolete accommodation at Shaughnessy hospital, Vancouver, is now nearing completion and the patients have been moved into this new accommodation. A similar replacement project has been started at Westminster hospital, London. Architects' plans are being prepared for the construction of a veterans pavillion in connection with the general hospital in St. John's, Newfoundland, and preliminary planning is now being done in the department for extensive alterations to Queen Mary veterans hospital, Montreal, and Ste. Anne's hospital at Ste. Anne de Bellevue.
As an instance of the lively interest taken by the members of the standing committee on veterans affairs in our hospital facilities I should mention that last year the committee visited Sunnybrook hospital, Toronto, and this year they expressed a wish to inspect 79951-0-426J
Supply-Veterans Affairs older accommodation in order that they might appreciate the problems faced by the department in providing treatment in obsolescent accommodation. Accordingly, on Wednesday May 25 the committee visited Queen Mary veterans hospital at Montreal and our institution at Ste. Anne de Bellevue. I understand they considered their visit most informative, as they got valuable firsthand information on the difficulties of providing first class modern treatment under somewhat difficult conditions.
The amount we expect to spend this year on hospital construction and improvements and equipment has been estimated at $4,937,000. The medical research and education features of our treatment services are expected to continue at the same level as last year, as are the prosthetic services offered by the department.
I should now like to say a few words with respect to the Veterans Land Act. As hon. members know, this act was amended last year. We now have some indication of the effects of the improvements in this legislation which the amendments brought about. These amendments increased the maximum amounts available to full time farmers to $20,000 and to small holders to $10,000, and in part II of the act housing assistance was raised to $10,000.
The greatest impact on the administration has been created by the amendments respecting full-time farmers. These will considerably increase the work load during the current year. It has been found necessary to make the staff fully familiar with the farm appraisal and loan principles which must be followed in order that the increased amounts may be invested wisely for the basic purposes for which they were intended, the acquisition or development of economic family farm units. The estimated cost of administration this year is nevertheless almost exactly the same as the total allotment for last year.
We found that after a slow start there was an increase of more than 25 per cent in the number of farm loans approved in the last nine months of 1959-60 over the previous year, and that financial assistance to small holders and commercial fishermen showed an increase in number of about 20 per cent over that experienced before the amendments. House construction continues at a fairly high level, with 1,436 new houses commenced, a slight reduction compared to the previous year, due in the main to veterans deferring their plans until after the amendments became effective. Our total investment last year for the purchase of land, buildings, livestock and farm machinery was about $2.5 million greater than in 1958-59. Our estimate for this item
