speechtext:
As the committee of the whole house had occasion to adjourn at six o'clock I was just beginning to discuss one of the statements made by the minister after I had occasion to make certain remarks on other matters he brought up in a statement which he had just previously had occasion to give the committee.
When a backbencher brings up questions concerning the development of our northern resources he is faced with the fact that he is discussing the northern vision of the


Conservative party which was on so many occasions expressed during the last two elections, and on this score the minister of northern affairs had occasion to tell the committee a few moments ago that the policies which he had occasion to bring about in the course of his functions in the last two or three years were about to be amended. All hon. members of the committee will recall that the minister often had occasion to make statements concerning the policy of the Conservative party and concerning the expansion and exploitation of our resources in the great north, and I find that the minister today possibly reminds me of a pair of trousers on a windy clothesline-there is a lot of vehement movement but it remains in the same position.
I call the attention of the committee to certain of the statements made as to the policies entertained by the minister of northern affairs, and what has become of them. The committee still realizes that those statements were numerous and the enunciations of policy were numerous, but this great vision of the Prime Minister and the minister of northern affairs has become a mere mirage and now we come to the third year since this government took office and the mirage is going away from us as we go on.
The hon. minister will agree with me that it is advisable to consider these problems in the same light as he asked members of the committee on mines and forests to do when last year he had occasion to present a report to that committee, at which time he set out his policies and gave us the bases on which the formula of this government should be based. I read from page 2 of that report. The minister will remember the report I am reading. He said this:
The government has two bases for its policies toward northern resources. We want firstly, to encourage their early exploration, later their development, and eventually their exploitation; and secondly we are determined to protect the public interest in them. Our policy in northern oil and gas should be judged on these bases. Let me give you some thoughts which illustrate how our policy meets this criteria.
I wish to discuss the policies of this government on these very same bases-how we are going to develop the north, and the measures we are going to take to develop our resources. Second, how are we going to protect the public interest of the Canadian people as far as our resources are concerned.
How were they expanded in the course of the operations of the minister of northern affairs? We were told that there was a great move, that there was an invitation for exploration accorded, and one read very recently after the expiration, after the minister

had extended the terms for these applications, an account of what happened. I should like to read a quotation to substantiate the position of this great promise of expansion by the Prime Minister and the minister of northern affairs. Here is what I read in the Financial Times of July 8 of this year. It is quite recent. The heading is "Arctic Reserves Sales Disappoint".
The final count of applications for oil and gas exploration permits in the Arctic islands turned out to have fizzled to barely a quarter of the sensational volume of acreage taken under temporary allocation a year and a half ago.
The devastating admission was made by Hon. Alvin Hamilton, Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources after the June 25 deadline for filing of formal applications for permits involving definite expenditures.
It is obvious from such a report that the promises made in this house and elsewhere by the minister of northern affairs do not live up to expectations. It was said that this government had begun, and was about to fulfil, a program of expansion of our resources as never before. I had occasion to check some of the figures in the estimates presented by the minister. I have indicated earlier some of the facts relating to the diminishing of the capital expenditure included in these estimates and also the rise in the cost of the administration. Now the minister could not possibly have told the committee how he had achieved the increase which the promise had indicated to the Canadian people. I should like to quote, to indicate the expansion suggested by the minister of northern affairs, an article which appeared in the Financial Post of July 9 of this year, which is also a recent article. This goes over the estimates which we are now about to discuss. It is comparing the dollars spent by the department with regard to what the previous government had occasion to introduce in its estimates with the amount spent by the present administration. The article is written by one Leslie Wilson, and it states:
The northern "vision", as defined by the Conservatives, was a big issue in the election of March, 1958, which gave the present government an overwhelming majority.
Do any differences in emphasis on northern development show up in the northern affairs budgets of the two governments? Here are the figures:
From 1953-54-the budget before the re-baptism-
That has reference of course to the fact that during the St. Laurent regime in 1954 the department of resources and development was made into the present department. The article continues:
-to the present, the department spending has increased by a cumulative annual 22.3 per cent.
For the Liberal, budgets, the growth rate is 26 per cent, for the'Conservative budgets, 16 per cent.
Supply-Northern Affairs
The committee surely will realize from these figures that the growth of the department was not under the Conservative government from what it had been since 1953 under the Liberal government.
The second statement the minister made was to the effect that this government had done something to reserve for Canadians their natural resources and to ensure Canadian participation in their exploitation. The minister made much fuss about the fact that he had taken action to ensure Canadian participation in the development of our natural resources. In a release issued by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources over the signature of the minister we find a statement to the effect that the regulations remain largely the same in detail but the two important clauses concerning Canadian participation have been added at the lease stage.
This is an admission on the part of the minister that the regulations except for the two additions to which he had reference have not been changed in any substantial way. His statement indicates that participation is only at the lease stage. Any company interested in exploration must first take out a permit. There is no protection provided to people interested in the exploitation of our resources.
The minister announced in the Canada Gazette in May, 1960 new regulations for mining and on June 22, 1960 he announced in that same publication new regulations concerning gas and oil leases. I will read the clause to which the minister referred, which provides that no lease shall be given to a company unless certain conditions are met. There are many clauses listed but the important one is at the end. It is contained in clause 32, subclause 2, paragraph 2. It provides that to obtain a lease the company must see to it that the shares of the corporation are listed on a recognized Canadian stock exchange and that Canadians will have an opportunity of participating in the ownership of the corporation.
The only way to obtain ownership in a corporation is to buy shares. To state that a company incorporated in Canada is to have its shares offered on the market means practically nothing to the people who are prepared to finance projects. To me this has about as much significance as would a regulation introduced by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, who I see is in the chamber this evening, to the effect that the government would be prepared to give a person full Canadian citizenship with all the attendant privileges if he were prepared to wear a Canadian-made suit. This regulation has roughly the same application.
6792	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs
I have not made a survey of all the companies that have bought leases covering the resources of Canada. The minister a few weeks ago was kind enough to make a statement in this chamber concerning certain companies that had such an interest. I will take one of these companies as an example and I intend my remarks to be no reflection on the company which is doing the best it can to explore and exploit resources in Canada. We in the opposition agree with this practice.	.
For the purposes of my illustration I will take the Cree Oil of Canada Limited. I will not take the smallest holder. The company has obtained 4,500,000 acres in a given project. According to the long list furnished by the minister it is the second largest holder. I attempted to ascertain who were the Cree Oil company and in what way it could be considered as a Canadian company. I did research in the book entitled, "Survey of Oils-1960" published by the Financial Post. This is a document of great interest and importance and is most complete. I looked up the Cree Oil company and found a notation to the effect that this company was formed in 1956 with all assets acquired by North Star Oil Limited effective December 15, 1958.
In order to discover the true situation and who has obtained leases on Canadian natural resources we go to the listing for North Star Oil Limited. It was a company formed in Canada, incorporated in 1919, according to this indisputably reliable report. The report indicates that Shell Oil acquired control in 1960 of class A and common shares of North Star Oil Limited held by the estate of the late F. C. Manning. These were purchased by Shell Oil Company of Canada Limited. The acquisition represented majority control in the company.
The minister indicated that this was a Canadian company but we find it is now owned by the Shell Oil Company. Is this a Canadian company? I do not know all the particulars. 1 realize that perhaps people in many parts of the world invest in Shell Oil Company. However, I suggest to the minister that he would do well to agree with statements made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, his colleague.
On July 4, 1960 the hon. member for Laurier directed a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, as reported at page 5655 of Hansard of that date, inquiring whether Canada had made any protest against the confiscation of the Shell Oil refinery in Cuba. On that occasion the following exchange occurred between the hon. member for Laurier and the Secretary of State for External Affairs:

Mr. Speaker, there has been no


protest made. It so happens that the real ownership of this refinery is in the United Kingdom and the Netherlands.
